segments.title: A long-range flying boat built on Blackburn's oversized aircraft experience
segments.summary: Blackburn drew on its earlier large-aircraft work when it began the R.B.1 Iris, a very large long-range reconnaissance flying boat designed to Air Ministry Specification R.14/24.
segments.body: The Iris opens as proof that Blackburn could produce a beautiful aircraft. The company drew on its experience with oversized aircraft structures from the Great Kookaburra air biplane. Work began in 1924 on a very large flying boat for long-range reconnaissance. Major J. D. Rennie designed the aircraft to Air Ministry Specification R.14/24. Its scale, flying-boat form, and reconnaissance role defined the design brief.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces the Iris, Blackburn's previous large-aircraft experience, its 1924 start, Rennie, and Specification R.14/24.

segments.title: Three engines for a safer overwater patrol
segments.summary: The Iris used three engines to reduce the danger of a forced descent at sea, retaining altitude at full load on two engines and remaining airborne after losing two.
segments.body: Engine redundancy gave the long-range flying boat a practical measure of safety over water. The Iris carried three engines specifically to reduce the risk of a forced descent at sea. It could maintain height at full load on any two engines, leaving near-normal flight available after one failure. Even after losing a second engine, the aircraft could keep going, though at a less desirable altitude. That reserve meant an engine failure far from shore did not have to become an immediate landing and survival emergency.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the three-engine arrangement, its forced-descent rationale, and the aircraft's performance after one or two engine failures.

segments.title: Hull form and the difficult transition to flight
segments.summary: The Iris combined a plywood-covered wooden hull with a sharp two-step V-bottom to run cleanly on the water and shorten the costly, demanding takeoff transition.
segments.body: The Iris used a plywood-covered wooden hull with a streamlined, sharp two-step V-bottom. Its clean run across the water helped the aircraft accelerate toward flying speed. During that transition the engines had to operate at full power, consuming fuel and placing strain on the airframe. Floating and airborne flight were relatively settled conditions, while takeoff and landing put greater demands on the aircraft. A quicker transition reduced fuel use and limited that strain. Only four were built, a number the closing line calls "cruelty" after praising the aircraft's beauty.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the Iris hull, explains why fast water acceleration matters for takeoff, and notes that only four aircraft were built.
